---
title: "Brain region mappings"
---

A mapping is a choice of how finely to describe anatomy. The Allen hierarchy has thousands of
regions; almost no analysis wants that many. A mapping picks a level of the
[structure tree](brain-region-hierarchy.qmd) and collapses everything below it.

## The four mappings

| Mapping | Regions | Use it when |
|---|---|---|
| **Allen** | 1328 | You want the full Allen parcellation; the default |
| **Beryl** | 308 | A middle granularity, the usual choice for brain-wide summaries |
| **Cosmos** | 12 | Coarse, major divisions only |
| **Swanson** | 319 | You are plotting on the Swanson flat map |

Cosmos is short enough to print in full: `void`, `root`, `Isocortex`, `OLF`, `HPF`, `CTXsp`,
`CNU`, `TH`, `HY`, `MB`, `HB`, `CB`.

Each has an `-lr` lateralised twin, so `br.mappings` holds eight keys in all. The plain
variant merges hemispheres; the `-lr` variant keeps them apart using the negative-id
convention. Allen has 1328 targets against Allen-lr's 2655; Swanson has 319 against
Swanson-lr's 645.

::: {.callout-note}
## Where Beryl and Cosmos come from is not documented

The package defines these mappings but records nothing about who drew them or on what basis.
Allen is the Allen Institute parcellation and Swanson follows the Swanson flat map, but the
provenance of Beryl and Cosmos is not stated anywhere in the code or the fixtures. Treat the
names as IBL conventions until someone can source them.
:::

## What a mapping actually stores

A mapping stores, for each of the 2655 regions, the **index of the highest-level ancestor that
should be considered**. Every region below that node is given its parent's annotation.

```python
br.mappings['Beryl']        # 2655 indices -> 308 distinct targets
br.mappings.keys()          # the eight mappings
```

So mapping is not lookup, it is collapse: `MOp1`, `MOp2/3`, `MOp5` and `MOp6a` all resolve to
whatever ancestor the mapping terminates at. Nothing is lost from the tree itself — the
mapping is a view over it.

## Swanson behaves differently, in three ways that catch people

The Swanson flat map is the signature figure of the brain-wide map papers, and it is the
mapping people hit problems with. Three behaviours are worth knowing before you plot.

### Only Swanson regions, or their parents, can be plotted

The flat map draws a fixed set of 319 regions. A region outside that set has nowhere to go.
Passing one does not raise — it is silently filled with `empty_color` (`'silver'` by default),
so a region quietly missing from your figure is the expected failure mode, not an error.

### A parent fills every Swanson region inside it

Pass a parent and its value propagates down to all its descendants, via
`BrainRegions.propagate_down`. `Isocortex` has 374 descendants, 40 of which are Swanson
regions — so one value for `Isocortex` colours 40 separate patches identically:

```python
idx, vals = br.propagate_down(np.array(['Isocortex']), np.array([1.0]))
len(idx)   # 374 descendants
```

This is useful when you mean it and misleading when you do not. A coarse region painted across
a wide area looks like 40 measurements rather than one.

### The mapping itself holds only one hemisphere

`br.mappings['Swanson']` contains **no negative ids at all** — it is a single hemisphere.
Only `Swanson-lr` carries both, with 322 negative entries.

Consequently a two-hemisphere display needs **signed Allen ids**, not acronyms: an acronym
such as `MOp` is identical on both sides and cannot express which one you mean. Note too that
`plot_swanson_vector` takes the absolute value of negative ids when `hemisphere` is anything
other than `'both'` — so passing signed ids with the wrong `hemisphere` argument silently
merges the sides.
